newsitem.title: GERMANY: Gibraltar sees firm interest as insurance centre.
newsitem.headline: Gibraltar sees firm interest as insurance centre.

text.p: Gibraltar is experiencing strong interest from insurance companies and captive managers now the final legal hurdles for its status as a European Union insurance centre have been cleared, Peter Montegriffo, deputy chief minister, told Reuters on Friday.

Montegriffo, who is taking part in the Cologne risk management conference, said: "We have had very interesting discussions with conference participants, and even before the final go-ahead came from the UK government, a number of parties made inquiries."

Reinsurers and insurers from South Africa, captive insurance operations from Germany, American insurance companies and insurers from other EU locations had shown interest in setting up their base in Gibraltar.
Captive insurance companies are special purpose insurance vehicles formed by large companies to insure their own or related risks.

This week, the London government confirmed that Gibraltar's supervisory regime was in line with that of the UK and thus with EU requirements. This makes it possible for Gibraltar-based insurers to write insurance business cross-border to all EU member states.
"Gibraltar has been a captive location for many years," said Montegriffo. At present, there were eight captives and insurers, mostly linked to UK companies.

"The difference now is that Gibraltar will be able to offer captives and other insurers an opportunity to write business directly into the EU without having to go through another insurer in an EU country."
"This comes in addition to services that places like Guernsey, the Isle of Man and Bermuda can also offer, but they do not have passporting."
Passporting is the ability to offer insurance across EU borders without having to have a separate local subsidiary.

Montegriffo said that so far, cross-border selling played only a minor role in EU insurance. "This is the same with cross-border work in investment services. But undoubtedly companies look at passporting rights as a further attribute of what they would like to do in the long term."
"We will compete mainly with Dublin and Luxembourg, which both have passporting and have in recent years gained considerable business with that argument," Gibraltar's deputy chief minister said.

"If it comes to the question of why Gibraltar and not Dublin, we would answer that we have a number of advantages, such as our tax regime. Dublin has a 10 percent level of tax until 2005, and although that period will probably be extended, the Gibraltar regime is a permanent feature and is set at between zero and 35 percent, at the company's choice."

"Secondly, we believe that we are more cost-efficient, with regard to office space and residential accommodation. Thirdly, we take a more liberal attitude when it comes to employment. Dublin insists on local employment quotas being met, Gibraltar doesn't make it a pre-condition for operators to use Gibraltarians."
The Gibraltar insurance supervision through the Financial Services Commission matched UK standards.

"But that does not mean, of course, that it will be the same regulation. For example, the UK requires a minimum capital for insurance companies, which is not required by European Union directives. Gibraltar does not have capitalisation requirements, we simply fall back on the solvency margins and guarantee fund set in the directive."
Montegriffo did not want to make a forecast of how the market would develop.

"We are long-term players in this industry. We won't measure our success by how many companies are attracted within a definite period of time. We are also interested primarily in quality over quantity. We would much rather have major players using Gibraltar rather than a large number of less important institutions."
